items.title: A small republic in every classroom
items.description: PAKISTAN is extraordinarily young. Two in every three of its people are under 30. The question is not whether Generation Z will change Pakistan. Demographically, it will. The question is whether it will be ready, and little in the way this country is arranged suggests it will. Their task can be stated in a sentence. The Constitution of Pakistan on paper and the Constitution as it works on the ground are two different documents, and the distance between them is what this generation has to close. I was 14 when martial law came and a young man when that general died. My generation learnt a dangerous lesson: power does not explain itself. The man who speaks out is transferred; the man who stays quiet is promoted; the judge who insists upon his independence is superseded. Caution, practised long enough, becomes accommodation, and accommodation becomes submission. We learnt to accommodate power. Our institutions learnt it too. The courts found a doctrine for every occasion: revolutionary legality in 1958, necessity in 1977, validation in 2000. Havel wrote of the greengrocer who displayed a slogan he did not believe because it was safer. Parties became family enterprises; student unions were banned in 1984 and never restored. What we built governs without consent. Pakistan’s next generation will not be formed by protest. It will be formed by argument, and the place to begin it already exists. So what must this generation build first? Not a movement. Character. I have watched men who stood fearlessly at the bar change after reaching the bench. Not suddenly, and not for money. The comfort of office begins quietly to weigh, and each surrender is called realistic. Character is what resists that, and character is built by exposure to lives larger than one’s own. That is what history, literature and poetry are for: to make suffering legible, so that conviction has something to rest upon. But reading alone will not do it. What is read must be argued about, and the structure for that argument is already built, already funded and sitting idle. It is the university classroom. Every class, in every discipline, should be run as a small republic, and the argument should be about the discipline itself. Let the law class argue whether a judgement was rightly decided, not merely what it held. Let the medical class argue triage, consent, and who receives the last bed in a public ward. Let the engineering class argue what was built, who paid, and who must live beside it. Let the business class argue what a wage ought to be, and whether a balance sheet that is lawful is therefore honest. Every syllabus buries such questions beneath what is examinable. Let each class elect its office bearers, for a fixed term and with real duties. Let the elections be contested, and let students lose them, because losing an election and returning next week to sit beside the person who beat you is the most useful hour of civic instruction this country could offer. Let the dissenter be protected by rule, not by the goodwill of the majority. That is how a democratic mind is made: by being outvoted by someone you believe wrong, and having to work beside him afterwards. Argue any of these questions honestly and it will not remain within its discipline. Ask an engineering class whether the dam should be built. The answer requires a lawyer on water rights, an economist on who bears the cost, a doctor on what happens downstream, and someone who has met the people being moved. A faculty can contain a syllabus; it cannot contain a real question. Memorisation keeps a student inside his discipline; argument drives him out. Debate and multidisciplinary education are not two reforms but one, and the first produces the second. This is also where the politics lies. Our professions are organised as separate estates: a bar, a medical association, a chamber of commerce. Each can be managed on its own. What cannot be managed is a generation of doctors, engineers, lawyers and accountants who argued with one another at 20 and still take one another’s calls at 40. Teaching without debate is not education. It is transmission. Education here needs revisiting at its root: less theory recited, more of it tested against the country outside. Take the law class to a district court, the medical class to a public ward at night, the engineering class to the settlement beside the project, the business class to the factory floor. Students must be made to feel Pakistan and its misery, not to read about it. Imagine the young men and women such an education would prepare. The more grounded they are, the more effective they will be. A generation formed this way will not need to be told to push back against unelected power. It will be too many, too competent and too well connected to be governed without consent. None of this arrives quickly. It takes two decades, the time between losing a class election at 20 and running a ministry or a court at 40. That is the honest horizon, and why the work must begin now. Return, then, to the gap. On paper the Constitution is not in doubt: authority exercised through the chosen representatives of the people, rights that power may not violate, public power exercised for the common good. My generation learnt to live inside the distance between that page and this country. Look at what we have brought it to. Closing that distance is the work now left to theirs. They must learn to hold power to account. It begins in a classroom, with an argument, and an election that somebody loses. The writer is a former senior puisne judge of the Supreme Court of Pakistan. He holds the Distinguished Chair in Constitutionalism & Justice at the Shaikh Ahmad Hassan School of Law, Lums, and is currently a Distinguished Visiting Fellow at Yale University. www.justicemansooralishah.com Published in Dawn, September 20th, 2026

items.title: 31 APC Govs vs wike: Tinubu faces difficult options
items.description: By Omeiza Ajayi Tension that had simmered for months within the All Progressives Congress, APC, and the immediate circle of President Bola Tinubu has finally spilled into full public view, setting the Minister of the Federal Capital Territory FCT, Nyesom Wike, against a bloc of governors elected on the party’s ticket, and raising hard questions about how the president plans to keep his disciples intact heading into the 2027 election. Where each side stands The governors staked out their position at a closed-door session of the Progressive Governors Forum PGF in Abuja last Monday, presided over by Imo State Governor, Hope Uzodimma. Accounts of that meeting indicate the forum resolved that the party would throw its weight behind official APC candidates alone, refusing to endorse anyone emerging from an outside coalition. Their reasoning centred on the fear that backing candidates beyond APC’s own fold would dilute the party’s strength, sow confusion among voters at the grassroots, and split loyalties within the ranks. Speaking on behalf of the group, Uzodimma warned that the party had no appetite for arrangements likely to fracture internal loyalty or put Tinubu’s second-term ambitions at risk. The governor’s fears might not be misplaced but it is simply about self-preservation and not for the love of the president. In the days of the defunct Alliance for Democracy AD when its governors agreed to work for the reelection of then President Olusegun Obasanjo, only Tinubu, as Lagos State Governor, survived the aftermath. His othe colleagues lost their states and Obasanjo became the greatest beneficiary. The governors are concerned that Wike’s rainbow coalition, of allowed to stand, could cause political mishaps for them. Wike has met the governors’ position with open defiance rather than any attempt at reconciliation. Appearing on Arise Television, he flatly denied ever seeking the governors’ endorsement for what his Rainbow Coalition, a grouping that pulls together politicians from rival parties who, by his account, are mobilising for Tinubu’s re-election rather than for the APC as an organisation. “There is no day I went to the Governors’ Forum to align with any rainbow coalition—there is no such day. I have never, one day, gone to the APC Forum for an alliance.” His pushback did not stop there; he went on to brand the governors as “politically lazy,” and compared their handling of the matter to fraudsters who talk big but lack any real strategy for delivering the president votes. The minister has also worked to place himself beyond the governors’ reach by invoking his direct relationship with the presidency. “There is nothing that I do that I don’t tell Mr President. I am not answerable to APC governors,” he said. How rift began This confrontation did not appear overnight. Political analyst Uche Igwe, traced its origins to the day Wike was named FCT minister, an appointment that unsettled long-standing power arrangements among Tinubu’s southern allies, where Wike and Uzodimma both wield considerable influence without necessarily pulling in the same direction. Wike himself has alluded to this. Denge Josef Onoh, a former South-East spokesman for Tinubu, has placed the present standoff within the broader sweep of Wike’s political history, pointing back to his role in the G5, a bloc of PDP governors who withheld their backing from the Peoples Democratic Party PDP’s Atiku Abubakar in 2023 after Wike’s own bid for the party’s presidential ticket fell to Atiku. Onoh contended that the episode ended up benefiting Tinubu by widening the cracks inside the PDP, a precedent he implies is worth watching as this fresh dispute plays out. What lit the fuse this time is the Rainbow Coalition project itself, which Wike has spent weeks publicly championing as his contribution to securing Tinubu a second term by pulling opposition figures into the president’s camp without asking them to formally defect. He has spoken of the coalition’s potential to keep expanding, citing Osun State Governor-elect Ademola Adeleke’s visit to the president as proof of a broadening political realignment. Yet it is exactly this openness to politicians outside the APC that troubles the governors, who see any Rainbow Coalition candidate elected under a different party’s banner as another seat lost to the opposition, regardless of how loyally the occupant or candidate may serve Tinubu personally. What is at stake for Tinubu A president preparing to seek re-election can ill afford an open clash between his governors and one of his most prominent ministers becoming public spectacle. The APC’s Presidential Campaign Council (PCC) has already sounded the alarm. One of its spokesmen, Ima Niboro, has warned that the standoff could damage the party’s fortunes in 2027 if it is allowed to fester, even while describing it as an internal disagreement among allies chasing the same objective. Tinubu faces a dilemma cutting both ways. The governors hold the levers of party structure, local government networks and, in many states, the grassroots machinery that actually turns out votes, resources that Wike, whatever his public profile, does not directly control across most of these states. Yet Wike has cast himself as the one broadening Tinubu’s appeal beyond the APC’s traditional base, drawing in politicians who might otherwise stay neutral or throw their support behind a rival. His development exploits in the Federal Capital Territory FCT is, arguably, the major bragging right of the ruling party. Whichever side ends up feeling sidelined, the cost will be real, and the governors’ formal rejection of the Rainbow Coalition, matched by Wike’s equally public refusal to answer to them, means this is no longer something Tinubu can allow to quietly work itself out. Has Tinubu stepped in, and where would he lean? So far, the president has kept his own counsel publicly, and that silence is precisely what has fuelled growing calls for him to step forward. Niboro’s appeal to the president, framed around Tinubu’s political experience and capacity to settle the matter internally, is itself an admission that no such intervention has yet materialised. Wike, meanwhile, maintains that Tinubu is already fully informed of his political moves and, by implication, sympathetic to his side, insisting there is nothing he undertakes politically without first briefing the president. Party opinion is already splitting along the same fault lines as the two principals. Former lawmaker Abdulmumin Jibrin has publicly rallied to Wike’s defence, saying the minister does not deserve to be publicly humiliated and arguing that virtually every APC member has, directly or indirectly, benefited from Wike’s role in delivering the president and running the affairs of government. Others, chiefly the governors themselves, appear to be banking on Tinubu ultimately favouring party discipline and structure over loyalty to a single minister, however valuable his contributions may be. What either choice would cost him If Tinubu comes down firmly on the governors’ side, compelling Wike to bring the Rainbow Coalition under strict APC control or to soften his public attacks on the PGF, he stands to alienate a minister who has been central to his political strategy in the South since 2023 and who has already demonstrated, through his G5 role that year, a willingness to damage a campaign from within when he feels disrespected. A sidelined Wike, denied the coalition project he has poured months of public effort into, becomes a far less predictable ally than one working in step with the president. Should Tinubu instead back Wike, effectively giving the Rainbow Coalition his blessing over the governors’ objections, he risks a different kind of fallout: a Progressive Governors Forum left feeling that its authority over party discipline has been overruled in favour of a minister who is not even a registered APC member. Since governors run the party apparatus in their respective states, a bruised PGF could quietly scale back enthusiasm on the ground come 2027, a subtler but no less damaging form of disengagement than an outright public revolt. Room for a middle path? The PCC’s description of the dispute, as a disagreement between allies working toward a shared goal, hints at the kind of compromise Tinubu is more likely to pursue than a decisive choice between the two camps. Such a settlement might involve the president acknowledging the Rainbow Coalition’s value to his re-election bid while insisting it stop short of fielding candidates directly against sitting APC officeholders, an arrangement that would let Wike keep his project alive while letting the governors keep their territory intact. Given Tinubu’s track record, illustrated by his earlier efforts to broker peace between Wike and Rivers State Governor Siminalayi Fubara, of favouring negotiated truces over blunt rulings, a similar brokered outcome between Wike and the PGF remains plausible, though it would require both camps to climb down from positions they have, so far, stated without much room for compromise. Why inaction carries its own risk Perhaps the greater danger lies in the president continuing to say nothing. Each day the standoff goes unaddressed, it calcifies into a public storyline of disunity within the APC just as the party heads into a contest it cannot afford to fight divided. Wike’s sharpening rhetoric, including accusations levelled at named governors over greed and political laziness, combined with the governors’ decision to formalise their rejection of the Rainbow Coalition through an official forum resolution, points to a rift that has moved well beyond private grumbling into a matter of public record ripe for exploitation by opposition parties. Left to fester, it also threatens to stall cooperation between the FCT minister and APC governors in states where their combined, if uneasy, efforts have previously proved necessary to deliver results for the president, precisely the sort of quiet structural damage that becomes far harder to undo once campaign season is in full swing than a dispute settled early and decisively. The onus is on the president. The post 31 APC Govs vs wike: Tinubu faces difficult options appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Killing over alleged blasphemy rocks Sokoto
items.description: • Cleric survives knife attack in mosque, worshipers kill assailant, probe stokes controversy By Musa Ubandawaki, Sokoto Tension has gripped parts of Sokoto metropolis following the stabbing of controversial Islamic cleric, Sheikh Musa Ayuba Lukuwa, shortly after he conducted the Jumu’at prayer at his mosque in the Mabera area of the metropolis. The September 11 incident has since assumed a wider dimension, with the alleged attacker losing his life in mob action, the state government ordering the closure of the mosque as a crime scene, security agencies commencing investigations and an advisory committee of Islamic scholars being constituted to examine the wider religious tensions surrounding the controversy. The development has also generated a fresh debate over religious freedom, the limits of religious expression, the sanctity of human life, mob justice and the appropriate institutional response to allegations involving sensitive religious matters. Police authorities said the incident occurred at about 1:50 p.m. shortly after the Friday congregational prayer, when an unidentified man allegedly attacked Lukuwa with a sharp knife. According to the Police Public Relations Officer, DSP Ahmad Rufa’i, the alleged assailant inflicted injuries on the cleric before he was overpowered by worshippers at the scene. The situation, however, took a deadly turn when the alleged attacker was reportedly beaten by a mob and later died from injuries sustained during the assault. The police subsequently confirmed that one person died in connection with the incident, while the circumstances surrounding the death of the alleged attacker remained subject to investigation. The identity of the deceased has also remained a matter of conflicting accounts, with early police accounts describing him as unidentified, while other accounts circulated a name that has not been independently established by the authorities. For that reason, the identity and personal background of the deceased should await official confirmation rather than be treated as established fact. Sheikh Lukuwa, meanwhile, was rushed to hospital following the attack and received medical attention for injuries sustained during the incident. ‘I am well’ The police later said the cleric had been treated and discharged from hospital, while Lukuwa himself subsequently appeared in a video in which he sought to reassure his followers that he was well. In the video, the cleric appealed directly to his followers and members of the public to remain calm and resist any action capable of aggravating the situation. “I am well and in good health,” Lukuwa was reported to have said while reassuring his supporters following his return from hospital. He also urged his followers not to allow anger arising from the incident to result in retaliation or further violence. The cleric reportedly thanked those who rallied around him during the attack, saying their intervention helped to protect him from what he described as a potentially more serious assault. His appeal for calm came at a time when emotions were already running high across sections of the metropolis following the incident and the controversy that preceded it. The controversy has been linked to allegations concerning remarks attributed to Lukuwa on sensitive religious issues, including comments relating to the parents of Prophet Muhammad (SAW), although the precise context and content of the alleged remarks remain matters being examined. Sokoto State Government subsequently moved to contain the situation by ordering the immediate closure of the Sheikh Musa Ayuba Lukuwa Jumu’at Mosque in Mabera. Crime scene The government declared the mosque a crime scene and ordered that it remain closed until further notice to allow the relevant authorities to conduct their investigation. “The Government has ordered the full investigation into the attack and killing at Musa Lukuwa Jumu’at Mosque, Mabera, and ordered the closure of the mosque, being the crime scene, till further notice,” the government said. The government’s decision effectively transformed the mosque from a place of worship into a secured investigative site, with security personnel deployed around the premises to prevent unauthorised access and possible further disturbance. As of Friday, the mosque remained locked, with security operatives stationed around the area as authorities sought to prevent any possible breakdown of law and order. The closure is also expected to enable investigators to examine the physical surroundings, establish the sequence of events and gather evidence concerning both the stabbing and the subsequent killing of the alleged assailant. Beyond the criminal investigation, the state government has also established a 14-member Advisory Committee of Islamic scholars and representatives of major Muslim organisations to examine the broader religious controversy. The committee is chaired by Malam Yahaya na Malam Boyi, Sarkin Malamai, while representatives of Izala in Kaduna and Jos, Tijjaniyyah, Qadiriyyah, Jama’atu Nasril Islam and the Sultanate Council are among those listed as members. The Commissioner for Religious Affairs, Malam Lawal Maidoki and Barrister Gandi Umar Muhammad, who serves as secretary, are also members of the committee. According to the government, the committee has been mandated to “critically examine the position of Shari’ah on the issues raised by Malam Musa Lukuwa and advise the Government accordingly.” The committee is expected to submit its report to the state government within 14 days, effectively giving it two weeks to examine the issues and make recommendations. The government said the broader objective was to examine the immediate and remote causes of the religious tensions and advise it on measures capable of protecting peace and religious harmony in the state. “The State Government has constituted a committee of Ulamas to examine the remote and immediate causes of such crisis and advise the Government on the appropriate measures to be taken in the interest of the State,” the government stated. The government also declared that it dissociated itself from anyone who might use religion as a pretext to disrespect Prophet Muhammad (SAW), his parents, household or companions. “The Government has dissociated itself from any person of any status that hides under the pretext of religion to undermine or disrespect the Holy Prophet Muhammad (PBUH), his parents, his household and his companions,” it stated. At the same time, the administration appealed to residents to avoid inflammatory statements and actions capable of undermining the peaceful coexistence in the state. “The Government has appealed to people in the state to desist from inciting statements that could jeopardize the peaceful coexistence that Sokoto is known for,” it added. The government further assured residents that it remained committed to protecting lives and property and maintaining public order throughout the state. The police have equally maintained that religious sentiments cannot provide justification for individuals or groups to take the law into their own hands. Commissioner of Police, CP Hayatu Hassan Shafa, appealed to residents to remain calm and cooperate with security agencies investigating the incident. The Police Command specifically warned against reprisals, inflammatory statements, provocative gatherings and other actions capable of transforming the incident into a wider religious or communal confrontation. The Command said residents should allow the law to take its course and report useful information to security agencies rather than attempting to administer punishment themselves. The warning is particularly significant given that the alleged attacker was reportedly killed before he could be subjected to formal investigation or judicial proceedings. Controversy Meanwhile, a fresh controversy has emerged over the composition of the government’s advisory committee following concerns raised by Mallam Murtala Bello Asada, a disciple of Sheikh Lukuwa. In a message titled ‘Wannan Shine Ƙarshen Rashin Adalci?’ — translated as ‘Is This the Height of Injustice?’ — Asada questioned whether the process could command confidence if individuals allegedly involved in longstanding disagreements with Lukuwa were part of determining the issues surrounding him. “How can justice be achieved if some of those who have a long history of disagreement with Mallam Musa Ayuba Lukuwa are given the responsibility of investigating him?” Asada asked. He argued that if the objective was genuinely to establish the truth, all parties should be given an opportunity to present evidence and participate in a transparent process. “If the real intention is to discover the truth, let there be evidence. Let us sit down and engage in a dialogue with dignity,” he said. Asada further declared: “The truth is not afraid of confrontation. Justice is not afraid of investigation.” His intervention has introduced another layer into an already sensitive controversy, with attention now focused not only on the incident itself but also on the credibility and public acceptance of the investigative process. The committee’s composition, however, includes representatives from several Islamic organisations and institutions, reflecting an attempt by the government to bring different strands of the Muslim community into the process. The allegation of bias made by Asada remains an allegation and has not, from the sources reviewed, been established as a finding against any member of the committee. The broader security investigation and the religious advisory process are therefore distinct but interconnected aspects of the government’s response: one concerns the circumstances of the stabbing and death of the alleged attacker, while the other concerns the religious controversy and its underlying tensions. For Sokoto residents, the immediate concern remains the prevention of further violence, particularly as Friday prayers approach again across the metropolis. The incident has heightened attention to security arrangements around major Jumu’at mosques, with community leaders and security agencies expected to work together to prevent renewed confrontation. The police have urged Islamic scholars, traditional rulers, community leaders, parents and other influential individuals to use their positions to calm their followers and discourage inflammatory reactions. The command has also stressed that anyone with relevant information should make it available to investigators rather than spreading unverified claims on social media. The events surrounding Lukuwa’s mosque have therefore placed Sokoto at a critical juncture where the response of authorities, religious leaders and residents could determine whether the incident remains an isolated criminal episode or develops into a broader crisis. The government’s closure of the mosque, the criminal investigation, the establishment of the 14-member advisory committee and the police appeal for restraint represent the principal official responses announced so far. For now, Sheikh Lukuwa has survived the attack and publicly appealed for peace, while the alleged attacker is dead and unable to give his account of what transpired. As investigations continue, the overriding challenge before Sokoto is to ensure that religious disagreement does not become a justification for violence and that allegations, however sensitive, are subjected to evidence, due process and responsible scholarly engagement. The usual Friday congregational prayer was not observed today in the Mosque as it remained locked and key with security Agents on guard as ordered by the state government. The unfolding crisis has thus become more than an incident involving one cleric and one alleged attacker; it has developed into a test of how a deeply religious society manages controversy while preserving human life, public order, religious harmony and confidence in lawful institutions. The post Killing over alleged blasphemy rocks Sokoto appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: En Allemagne, un nouveau succès de l’AfD aux élections régionales pourrait faire tomber Merz
items.description: Deux semaines après les élections en Saxe-Anhalt qui ont vu le parti d’extrême droite AfD obtenir un score record, les électeurs allemands de Mecklembourg-Poméranie-Occidentale et de Berlin se rendront aujourd’hui aux urnes afin d'élire les 71 députés de la 9e législature du Landtag et les 130 députés de la 20e législature de la Chambre des députés, respectivement. Selon les derniers sondages, l’AfD est en tête des intentions de vote à Mecklembourg-Poméranie-Occidentale, avec 36,5 % (soit +19,8 points par rapport au scrutin précédent), suivi par le SPD (33,3 %). La CDU chute à 7 %, soit une baisse de 7 points par rapport à 2021. Si elle arrivait en tête, l’AfD serait toutefois à court d’une majorité (fixée à 36 sièges). À Berlin, Die Linke est en tête des intentions de vote (20,7 %), suivi par la CDU à 20 % et l’AfD à 17,9 %. L'élément important à observer à Berlin est de savoir si la gauche sera en mesure, à l'issue du vote, de former une coalition qui n'inclut pas la CDU. Le scrutin revêt une importance cruciale pour le chancelier Merz, qui, avec un taux de popularité particulièrement bas – dans un récent sondage 81 % des personnes interrogées jugent son action négativement –, fait face, 16 mois seulement après son arrivée au pouvoir, à une opposition croissante au sein de son propre parti. Les deux élections s'annoncent en effet difficiles pour la CDU, qui pourrait descendre proche du seuil de 5 % en Mecklembourg-Poméranie-Occidentale. Un tel résultat renforcerait considérablement la pression sur le chancelier Merz, qui a pour le moment exclu une possible démission. Toutefois, dans un tel scénario, un départ sous la contrainte du leadership de la CDU n'est pas à exclure. Si le ministre-président de la Rhénanie-du-Nord-Westphalie, Hendrik Wüst, et Markus Söder, ministre-président de la Bavière, sont présentés comme des candidats potentiels à la chancellerie pour remplacer Merz, ils devraient, si ce scénario se concrétise, réunir une majorité de voix au Bundestag, ce qui n'est pas garanti pour aucun successeur potentiel aujourd'hui. Si Merz démissionne et qu'aucun candidat ne rassemble suffisamment de voix au Bundestag, le président allemand pourrait convoquer des élections anticipées, une solution que la CDU/CSU, mais aussi le SPD, souhaitent éviter à tout prix. Huit ministres-présidents des Länder, dont Wüst, écrivent dans une lettre signée mercredi que l’Allemagne a besoin de stabilité, faisant référence directement aux élections nationales à venir l’année prochaine en France, en Italie, Grèce en Espagne et en Pologne : « Il sera donc d’autant plus crucial de pouvoir compter sur une Allemagne stable et forte au sein d’une Europe unie. » Solidarität mit #Merz . Die Ministerpräsidenten der CDU stützen den Kanzler. Diese Erklärung sei nicht über Nacht entstanden, höre ich @POLITICOEurope pic.twitter.com/UmowFlNnbM — Rasmus Buchsteiner (@R_Buchsteiner) September 16, 2026 Le ministre-président de la Bavière Markus Söder n’a pas signé la lettre. L’article En Allemagne, un nouveau succès de l’AfD aux élections régionales pourrait faire tomber Merz est apparu en premier sur Le Grand Continent .

items.title: An eye on Balochistan border
items.description: THE intensifying Yemeni Houthi strikes on Saudi Arabia have triggered a debate over the possible activation of the Makkah accord . Statements and clarifications about possible and emerging scenarios are coming from all stakeholders. But a recent incident in Saravan county in Sistan-Baluchestan, close to the Pakistan border, has also drawn attention to the Iran-Pakistan border region. This has broadened the debate over the Gulf region’s security and evolving geopolitics, and Pakistan’s role in it. The incident was reported on Sept 12, when heavy fighting between Iranian security forces and unidentified gunmen spread across parts of Saravan, with reports of attacks on military vehicles and dozens of security personnel killed or wounded. Although the identity of the armed group is not yet clear, some analysts have attributed the attack to Jaish al-Adl or the People’s Fighters Front, an alliance of several groups, reportedly including Jaish al-Adl. Since the start of the conflict in West Asia, Balochistan’s security dynamics have changed. The conflict has altered the operating environment in which an existing insurgency was already functioning. The BLA and other allied groups have intensified their terrorist activities . The economic blockade announced by these groups has disrupted transportation and halted economic activity, particularly in the mineral sector. The closure of the frontier with Afghanistan and the partial closure of the border with Iran have contributed to the crisis. Taken together, these developments have affected the region’s security, internal political dynamics and geopolitical environment, bringing new risks to the province. An angle that has largely been overlooked in the broader conflict theatre in this area is the state of affairs along the Pakistan-Iran border, which stretches for around 900 kilometres and where multiple violent religious and nationalist insurgent groups, as well as transnational criminal networks, operate. The border’s porous nature raises further security concerns. According to media reports, Pakistani security institutions had placed Balochistan on high alert because of the possible fallout from the Iran war. The situation along the Pakistan-Iran border in the broader conflict has been largely overlooked. The Jan 16, 2024, Iranian strike inside Pakistan , allegedly targeting Jaish al-Adl hideouts, followed by Pakistan’s retaliatory strikes on militant targets in Iran, changed the dynamics of their bilateral relations and prompted greater security cooperation. That cooperation has largely remained intact. However, the recent Saravan attack has raised questions about how the changing regional environment could affect the future course of frontier security, particularly as Pakistan’s border with Afghanistan remains closed and Iran is an alternative, although very expensive, route for transnational trade. For Iran, if the Revolutionary Guard (IRGC) has to concentrate its resources on US and Israeli strikes, the Strait of Hormuz and operations in the Gulf, Sistan-Baluchestan could become a per­ipheral theatre competing for Iranian security resources. Any escalation of tensions betw­een Iran and Pakistan is in neither country’s interest. However, non-state actors always try to find an opportunity in evolving conflicts, especially when wider regional contexts provide them with more meaning and relevance in the conflict theatre. The BLA and other insurgent groups appear to have viewed the war as an opportunity to escalate their operations, perhaps hoping that they could eventually be considered as potential proxies against Iran, as happened in Syria with America’s partnership with the Syrian Demo­cratic Forces. The SDF was a coalition that included Kurdish armed groups such as the YPG and YPJ, along with Syrian Arab and Assyrian/ Christian elements. The BLA has also issued a few statements supporting US strikes on Iran. Perhaps the BLA believes it can find meaning in the wider conflict in West Asia. Still, the BLA is missing a point in its calculation: the convergence of US, Pakistani, and Saudi geopolitical and strategic interests will persist in the coming years. At the same time, Jaish al-Adl and several smaller groups have reportedly sought to broaden their activities against the Quds Force and IRGC. The group remained relatively quiet until Iranian security forces launched an operation against suspected terrorists in Saravan last August, reportedly apprehending several Jaish al-Adl members and killing one. During the operation, security forces said they recovered a significant arsenal of military hardware, including dozens of Kalash­nikov automatic rifles, hand grenades, RPG-7 launchers, around 20 kilograms of C-4 military-grade explosives, 150 rounds of ammunition, and several Starlink satellite internet devices. The Saravan operation reported last week has since been interpreted in multiple ways, mostly based on assumptions rather than established evidence. One popular theory links the attack to the intensification of Houthi strikes on Saudi Arabia. The incident also occurred while Pakistan was diplomatically engaged with Iran. According to a media report, subsequently denied by Pakistan, Islamabad had conveyed a Saudi message to Tehran asking Iran to restrain the Houthis. A popular perception in the border region of Balochistan is that if Iran can use the Houthis as a proxy against Saudi Arabia, it must also expect the possibility of a similar reaction from Saudi Arabia. The Sunni militias operating in Sistan-Baluchestan, from Jundullah to the People’s Fighters Front, are said to be proxies of foreign powers including the US and Saudi Arabia. That perception is nurturing new theories. A few of them are critical of Pakistan too. Whether such perceptions translate into an actual Saudi strategy is another question. But perceptions themselves can influence the behaviour of armed groups and local actors, particularly in a region where terrorist networks, cross-border tribal connections and informal economic networks overlap. Beyond all the theories surrounding the strategic calculus of West Asia and the prospects of Saudi proxies emerging along the Pakistan-Iran border, one fact remains clear: Pakistan cannot afford further chaos in the border region of Balochistan. Any expansion of the regional conflict in an already fragile security environment could make the country’s internal security dynamics considerably more complex. The writer is a security analyst. Published in Dawn, September 20th, 2026

items.title: ‘High flood to hit Delta, Imo, Cross River, 12 other states in 7 days’
items.description: By Gabriel Ewepu The Nigeria Hydrological Services Agency, NiHSA, has warned of a high riverine flood risk across 15 states from September 19 to 25, 2026, urging affected communities to relocate to safer and higher grounds. The Director-General and Chief Executive Officer of NiHSA, Arch Umar Mohammed, disclosed this on Saturday in the agency’s National Flood Advisory. Mohammed said rising river levels were expected to cause flooding in several communities, with schools, healthcare facilities, markets, farms and religious buildings among those exposed. He urged affected state governments to urgently relocate residents in vulnerable communities to safer and higher grounds ahead of the predicted flooding. He said: “High riverine flood risk is forecast for the next seven days across Imo, Cross River and 13 other states. Rising river stages are expected to cause flooding. “Communities on the floodplain should prepare to move to higher ground. Stations include Obubra, Itigidi and Epento on the Cross River.” In Imo State, the affected local government areas are Aboh-Mbaise, Ahiazu-Mbaise, Ehime Mbano, Ezinihitte, Ideato North, Ihitte/Uboma and Ikeduru. The agency identified 958 communities, 1,022 schools, 553 healthcare facilities, 161 markets and 198 religious buildings as exposed. In Cross River State, the affected LGAs are Abi, Akamkpa, Akpabuyo, Biase, Calabar, Calabar South, Ikom and Obubra. NiHSA identified 2,471 communities, 703 schools, 344 healthcare facilities, 145 markets, 453 religious buildings and 854 hectares of farmland as exposed. In Ebonyi State, Abakaliki, Afikpo, Afikpo South, Ebonyi, Ezza North and Ezza South LGAs are affected. The exposure includes 2,574 communities, 1,064 schools, 422 healthcare facilities, 480 markets, 629 religious buildings and 1,882 hectares of farmland. In Benue State, Buruku, Gboko, Guma, Katsina-Ala, Logo and Ukum LGAs are affected, with 303 communities, 100 schools, 48 healthcare facilities, 32 markets, 151 religious buildings and 55 hectares of farmland exposed. In Anambra State, the affected LGAs are Aguata, Anambra East, Anambra West, Anaocha, Awka North, Awka South and Ayamelum. NiHSA identified 1,314 communities, 1,308 schools, 1,089 healthcare facilities, 280 markets, 610 religious buildings and 1,529 hectares of farmland as exposed. In Akwa Ibom State, Abak, Eket, Etinan, Ibeno, Ibesikpo Asutan, Ibiono Ibom, Ika and Ikono LGAs are affected. The agency listed 249 communities, 323 schools, 211 healthcare facilities, 74 markets and 289 religious buildings among the exposed assets. NiHSA also listed Edo, Bayelsa, Enugu, Kogi, Delta, Abia, Taraba, Rivers and Lagos among the other states facing severe flood risks during the forecast period. items.title: Petrol, gas: Cost of living spikes
items.description: Wage awards, palliatives no solution, analysts warn •Demand structural solutions, targeted relief for vulnerable people •LCCI seeks more crude for local refineries By Nnamdi Ojiego As the rising cost of living continues to pressure households and businesses across the country, economic, financial and social analysts have warned that wage awards and palliatives alone cannot resolve the crisis. The analysts said immediate relief may be necessary for vulnerable Nigerians, but argued that lasting solutions require lower transportation, energy, food, housing and other essential costs. Their positions followed renewed calls by the Nigeria Labour Congress, NLC, for wage awards and palliatives to cushion the impact of rising petrol prices. NLC, in a statement titled “Save the Situation Now,” signed by its President, Joe Ajaero, on Wednesday, said petrol now sells for about N1,430 per litre in major cities, with prices reportedly higher in less accessible locations. The labour centre said rising petrol prices would worsen transportation costs and trigger further increases in food, rent, school fees and other essential goods and services. “As a nation, and as a people endowed with enormous fossil resources, we are deserving of a certain level of protection or buffer against the gales from the Gulf, and indeed, other gales. “There is nothing wrong with government subsidising the needs of citizens, especially in emergency situations like this. On a long-term basis, we are equally concerned that local refineries are importing crude. This is unreasonable and unacceptable and defeats the logic and purpose of local capacity,” the statement said. Energy pressure The latest movement in energy prices illustrates the pressure already being transmitted through the economy. The price of cooking gas has risen by 25 per cent to between N1,500 and N1,600 per kilogramme from N1,200, while diesel prices have climbed to as high as N2,300 per litre at some filling stations. The September 16, 2026 mid-day depot price report showed sharp increases in diesel prices, particularly in Lagos and Port Harcourt. In Lagos, Ibachem recorded the biggest increase, with AGO rising from N1,830 to N2,000 per litre, while Ibeto increased from N1,835 to N1,970. Duport and Integrated rose by N110 each to N1,940 per litre. Ardova increased its AGO price by N20 to N1,970, while Eterna and Rain Oil sold at N2,000. Nipco was at N1,950. In Port Harcourt, African Terminal, Duport and Integrated increased their AGO prices by N110 each to N1,940, while Matrix in Warri raised its price from N2,080 to N2,120 per litre. Higher diesel prices are particularly significant for manufacturers, transport operators, telecommunications companies, small businesses and other users that depend on diesel for power, transportation and other operations. Petrol prices, meanwhile, remained relatively stable in some markets, ranging from N1,350 to N1,400 per litre in Lagos, with some reductions recorded in Calabar and Warri. Vice President of the Oil and Gas Service Providers Association of Nigeria, OGSPAN, Lawal Kamaldeen, said the volatility was likely to persist. “The downstream sector has been very unstable, characterised by frequent leaps in prices due to the prolonged USA-Iran war. Prices are likely to continue to be unstable in the coming weeks,” he said. Households under pressure For many households, the rising cost of essentials has translated into reduced spending, smaller food purchases and postponed needs. Abimbola Gbadamosi, a painter, said the rising cost of food, transportation and accommodation had put severe pressure on her income. “Honestly, coping with the spike in the cost of living has become increasingly difficult. The high prices of food, transportation, accommodation and other basic needs have put serious pressure on the meagre income I make from my painting business. “I have had to cut down on non-essential spending, prioritise basic needs and plan every expense carefully. Until there is greater stability in the prices of food, fuel, transportation and other essentials, many families will continue to struggle,” she said. For 28-year-old motor mechanic, Kareem Ayodele of Ado-Ekiti, the economic situation has forced him to postpone his marriage plans. “I had thought that before the end of this year, I would marry my fiancée, with whom I have been in a relationship for six years. But I have had to put it on hold because the traditional marriage requirements are beyond my budget,” he said. A teacher, Matthew Babatope, said food, rent, transportation and school expenses had become increasingly difficult to afford. He said a three-bedroom flat in remote parts of Akure now costs at least N400,000, while a plate of rice in some cafeterias sells for about N2,000. School fees, books and other expenses had also added to the burden on families. A petty trader in Ado-Ekiti, Janet Ibikunle, said rising wholesale prices had reduced her ability to restock. “Before, I could use a certain amount to buy enough goods and still make a little profit. Now, the money is not enough to buy the quantity I used to buy. “If I increase my price too much, customers will complain, but if I don’t, there is hardly any profit,” she said. Difficult to save A civil servant, Mr Bolu, said his unchanged income had also made it difficult to support friends and relatives who increasingly turn to him for financial assistance. “Unfortunately, my income has not changed. It has become difficult to save money because responsibilities are waiting to be attended to,” he said. He added that rising transportation and cooking gas costs had further reduced household purchasing power, with transport to school for his children rising from N500 to N700. Another civil servant, Segun Oloyede, said transportation alone consumed a significant part of his income. “My income has not increased in the same way that the prices of food, transport and other necessities have increased. These days, my salary seems to finish almost as soon as it comes,” he said. Oloyede said he now buys smaller quantities, reduces unnecessary spending and postpones some expenses to cope. For Folake Ajibola, a single mother of three, feeding her children has become one of her biggest challenges. “I have had to reduce the quantity of food I buy and, sometimes, change what I cook because I simply cannot afford some of the things we used to eat regularly,” she said. Ajibola said transportation, school expenses, electricity and healthcare costs had also forced her to prioritise one need over another. Mr Lanre Adegboyega of Owode, Ogun State, said he had also cut unnecessary spending, limited movement and compared prices before making purchases. Elder Ogundeyi Olufemi, a community leader, said his family had been forced to reduce food consumption because of falling purchasing power, while higher rent, electricity, transportation and cooking gas costs had added to the burden. He said the pressure was so severe that he was considering leaving his salaried job and relocating his family to their farm in the village to reduce household expenses. In Abakaliki, Ebonyi State, Mr Onuabuchi Nwite said many low-income families were finding it difficult to send their children back to school because of rising costs. “With the recent increase in fuel price, a poor man cannot afford transport fare and has resorted to trekking to various destinations. Some of my children have not resumed school because of lack of money to pay school fees, buy books and meet other expenses for the first term. Another resident, Mrs Chinwe Ogba, said women were bearing a significant share of the hardship because of the pressure of meeting household needs. “The cost of living is now beyond every average person in this country, not only in Ebonyi. There is no hope again because things keep deteriorating daily without any solution to the problem. “We are being choked by harsh policies, high taxes and increases in petroleum pump prices, leading to higher transport fares. Eventually, everything in the market has increased astronomically without any solution in sight. We only trust in God for our daily survival,” she said. Structural solutions Against this backdrop, Chief Executive Officer of the Centre for the Promotion of Private Enterprise, CPPE, Dr Muda Yusuf, said the current pressures required urgent intervention but cautioned against a return to universal petrol subsidy. According to him, relief should address the sources of household vulnerability and high business costs rather than subsidising petrol consumption indiscriminately. Yusuf said priority should be given to mass transit and logistics, improved electricity and alternative energy, food production, targeted social protection, healthcare and education, as well as measures to reduce energy, logistics and financing costs for businesses, particularly MSMEs. He said the government must ensure that additional revenues from subsidy removal translate into visible improvements in citizens’ welfare. “Citizens must see tangible benefits through improved public transportation, electricity, healthcare, education, food security, infrastructure and social protection,” Yusuf said. He added that the issue had increasingly become one of fiscal accountability and expenditure quality, stressing that governments should transparently demonstrate how additional fiscal resources were improving economic and social outcomes. “The more consequential issue is how Nigeria can convert the gains of the reform into lower structural costs, stronger domestic production, improved competitiveness, greater energy security and measurable improvements in citizens’ welfare,” he said. Long-term solution The President of the Lagos Chamber of Commerce and Industry, LCCI, Leye Kupoluyi, called for increased domestic refining to reduce fuel-price pressures. Kupoluyi said the Chamber had consistently advocated supplying more crude oil to local refineries so that more petroleum products could be refined locally and paid for in naira. “The Chamber has consistently advocated for the supply of more crude to the local refineries so we have more fuel refined locally and in local currency,” he said. He expressed reservations about previous social protection programmes, saying, “The negative reports on previous social protection interventions, such as cash transfers, cast doubt on the positive impact of such programmes.” The LCCI president said the business community had also opposed subsidising consumption instead of supporting production. “We have also spoken against subsidising consumption rather than intervening in production. The cost of living and the cost of doing business are reaching unbearable levels and definitely need immediate interventions,” Kupoluyi said. He identified fuel prices as a major source of pressure, saying, “Most cost and price pressures are driven by high fuel prices, including petrol, diesel, and jet fuel.” For the long term, he said Nigeria must reduce its exposure to external shocks. “The real long-term solution is to devise ways to avoid shocks from global markets and disruptions to global supply chains. We need to work together to put more pressure on the government to do the needful in a timely manner. “We reiterate our position that we need a local solution to the oil price crisis threatening economic activities, and that this should not be left unattended at this time,” he stated. Fixing the country Financial and social analyst, Blessing Iloh, said wage awards and palliatives could provide only temporary relief unless the underlying problems were addressed. “In all honesty, except for situations like COVID, palliative and wage awards usually provide temporary relief,” she said. Iloh said the NLC should instead push for the implementation of earlier promises on cheaper transportation and improved infrastructure, while identifying food production as an urgent priority. “Improved security that would allow farmers go back to farm. Honestly, if we have food like other countries do, we won’t be chasing wage awards just because of a temporary increase in oil prices,” she said. She also called for affordable credit and government-backed financing for solar power systems to reduce household and business energy costs. “Nigeria needs to stop being reactive. We need to fix this country once and for all. We must stop pretending to be fixing the country and show workings,” she said. The analyst argued that increasing workers’ pay without addressing the costs of housing, food, transport and other essentials would leave much of the problem unresolved. “Paying more money to workers without fixing the country is same as printing more naira notes. You cannot fix a country with more money. You fix it by addressing what caused the problem,” she said. •Additional reports by Dayo Johnson, Rotimi Ojomoyela, James Ogunnnaike, Jeff Agbod and Deola Badru The post Petrol, gas: Cost of living spikes appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: 37 miners’ suffocation: Anger spreads, 20 security officers suspended, mining disasters rock Kogi, Taraba
items.description: •Atiku, senators, others seek probe •Adeyanju speaks on alleged cover-up By Omeiza Ajayi, Luminous Jannamike Anger mounted yesterday over the reported deaths of 37 suspected illegal miners in the custody of the Niger State Command of the Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps, NSCDC, as the Federal Government suspended 20 officers and ordered an independent investigation into the circumstances surrounding the deaths. Specifically, government constituted a 10-member independent committee to investigate the incident. The action followed President Bola Tinubu’s directive for a comprehensive, transparent and unhindered investigation into the incident, which occurred on Thursday, September 17, 2026. Minister of Interior, Dr Olubunmi Tunji-Ojo, who announced the measures yesterday, described the deaths as deeply disturbing, saying government owed the families of the deceased and the Nigerian public a transparent account of what happened. The minister directed the suspension of all officers connected with the incident pending the outcome of the investigation and warned the leadership of the Corps against interfering with the process. He said: “Any attempt to destroy or conceal evidence, intimidate witnesses or obstruct the investigation will be treated as a serious offence.” The minister also directed the NSCDC leadership and all relevant officers to cooperate fully with the committee and preserve all records and material evidence connected with the incident. He consequently appealed for calm while the independent committee conducts its assignment. Probe The committee is mandated to establish the identities of the deceased and investigate the circumstances surrounding their arrest, detention and deaths. It is also expected to determine responsibility, complicity, negligence and misconduct, and recommend appropriate action, including compensation where applicable and measures to prevent a recurrence. The committee, which has two weeks to submit its report, is chaired by retired Deputy Director-General of the Department of State Services, DSS, Jonathan Kure, while a former Director-General of the Nigerian Law School, Prof. Isa Hayatu Chiroma, SAN, is secretary. Other members are retired AIG Hosea Hassan Karma; Prof. Olayinka Buhari, a professor of histopathology and former Chief Medical Director of the University of Ilorin Teaching Hospital; representatives of the Minna Emirate Council and Niger State Government; National Secretary of the Miners Association of Nigeria, Alhaji Liman Sulaiman; human rights lawyer, Deji Adeyanju; Mrs Zainab Suleiman Okino of Blueprint Newspaper; and public affairs analyst, Dr George Agbakahi. The committee may also co-opt relevant experts, access facilities and documents, visit locations connected with the incident and request memoranda from members of the public. Among the suspended officers, in addition to the Niger State Commandant of the NSCDC, Suberu Siyaka Aniviye, are officers involved in arrest, investigation, legal, and custodial duties. Officers They include SC Usman Isah Ndamaka; ASCI Hassan Mohammed; CCA Bala Mohammed; CSC Oluwadare Sunday; DCC Obafemi Elvis; CSC Annas Shitto Lamino; DCC Philip Ajayi; Barr. Stephen Tsado; ASCI Alhassan Mohammed; IC Abdullahi Sale; IC Mohammed Sonfada; CAI Liman Abubakar; CAI Bala Usman; IC Mohammed Jiya; DSC Isah Suleiman; CAI Ahmed Wushishi; IC Sale Adamu; IC Haruna Mohammed; ASCI Aliyu Sallah and CAI Isah Sanusi. Government, however, made it clear that the suspension of the affected officers is pending the outcome of the investigation and is not, in itself, a determination of their culpability. It maintained that the investigation must establish what happened and determine responsibility where wrongdoing is found. Sunday Vanguard learnt that the investigation is expected to examine the arrests, detention conditions, medical attention provided to the detainees and the events leading to their deaths, while also determining whether any official misconduct, negligence or other violations occurred. Reacting to his membership of the panel, Adeyanju said he would not accept any financial benefit from the assignment. The activist, who confirmed his acceptance of the appointment, said he joined the committee to ensure that the interests of the victims were protected and the circumstances surrounding their deaths established. Monetary He urged government not to make monetary provisions, stipends or honoraria for members of the committee, describing the assignment as a national duty. “I will not accept any such payment, and I will not participate in or tolerate any attempt to compromise the investigation or cover up wrongdoing,” he said. Adeyanju said he would personally bear the cost of his participation, including accommodation, transportation and other expenses. He further warned that any attempt to shield those responsible or suppress the truth would be exposed. “If there is any attempt to shield those responsible or suppress the truth, I will expose it,” he said. According to him, the victims deserved justice and the investigation must not be allowed to fall victim to what he described as the “Nigerian factor”. Deployed In a related development, NSCDC has deployed Abdulhamid Kabara as its new Commandant in Niger State. Kabara’s deployment followed the suspension of Suberu Aniviye as commandant of the Niger NSCDC Command. NSCDC spokesperson in the state, Abubakar Muti, said in a statement, yesterday, that Kabara formally assumed office and took over the leadership of the command on Friday, September 18. “The assumption of office comes at a particularly sensitive period for the Command, following the unfortunate deaths of some persons arrested in connection with suspected illegal mining activities in the State,” the statement said. Muti said Kabara expressed “deep sadness over the loss of lives and extended his heartfelt sympathy to the families of the deceased and everyone affected by the unfortunate incident.” Unacceptable Reacting to the incident, former Vice President Atiku Abubakar said the issue goes beyond the suspension of officers already announced by federal government. He said Nigerians must know how 37 people who entered government custody alive ended up dead and who, within the chain of command, should answer for their fate. Atiku, who stated this in a statement by his Senior Special Assistant on Public Communication, Phrank Shaibu, accused government of attempting to reduce a major accountability question to the suspension of junior personnel. “Thirty-seven Nigerians, many of them teenagers, entered government custody alive. Thirty-seven of them died there. The Tinubu administration cannot explain away 37 bodies with press releases, suspensions and bureaucratic excuses,” Atiku said. Atiku also challenged the Minister of Solid Minerals, Dele Alake, over enforcement operations in the mining sector, while saying Tinubu could not distance himself from the conduct of agencies under his administration. Tragedy “President Tinubu bears ultimate responsibility for the conduct of his government. He cannot behave like a spectator whenever his administration is confronted by tragedy, scandal or failure,” Atiku said. He demanded an independent criminal investigation into allegations that the detainees were held in an overcrowded, poorly ventilated cell, insisting that the probe must establish who authorised the operation, who ordered the arrests, how many people were detained and who was responsible for their welfare. “That allegation demands an immediate and independent criminal investigation. It cannot be resolved through an internal inquiry in which government officials investigate government agents and present government-approved conclusions to Nigerians,” he said. Atiku also called for the preservation of detention registers, operational and communication records, medical reports and available surveillance footage, as well as independent autopsies and representation for the victims’ families. The former Vice President linked the tragedy to the wider pressures driving young Nigerians into illegal mining, arguing that enforcement must not strip suspects of their rights. “Illegal mining is robbing Nigeria of its resources, destroying communities and threatening national security. It must be confronted firmly. But fighting illegal mining is not a licence for state agents to arrest citizens alive and return their bodies to their families,” he said. He recalled the 2014 Nigeria Immigration Service recruitment tragedy, when at least 16 job seekers died, and questioned why the standard of accountability should be different in the present case. “In 2014, at least 16 young Nigerians died during the Nigeria Immigration Service recruitment tragedy. The supervising minister, Abba Moro, was investigated and subsequently prosecuted over matters arising from that exercise. Why should the standard be different today?” Atiku asked. Deaths Senators from 19 Northern states and the Federal Capital Territory (FCT), under the aegis of the Northern Senators Forum, NSF, called for an independent, thorough and transparent investigation into the deaths. A statement by the Chairman of Northern Senators Forum, Senator Abdulaziz Musa Yar’adua, APC, Katsina Central, said:”The Northern Senators Forum joins the nation in mourning the reported deaths of 37 young Nigerians in the custody of the Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps (NSCDC) in Minna, Niger State. The circumstances surrounding their deaths, in which they were reportedly confined in a small room and cried for help before they choked to death, are deeply disturbing and unacceptable. “No Nigerian, regardless of the allegation against him, should lose his life in the custody of an agency established to protect lives and property. The sanctity of human life and the dignity of every person in custody must be upheld at all times. “The Northern Senators Forum therefore demands an immediate, transparent and independent investigation into the entire chain of events. Nigerians must know who ordered the arrests, where the detainees were taken, who authorised their detention in the facility, whether the room was fit for human habitation, when the distress calls were made, who heard them, what action was taken, and the precise circumstances in which each victim died. The investigation should involve the National Human Rights Commission, the Nigerian Bar Association, credible civil society organisations and independent forensic experts. “We equally demand independent autopsies for all 37 victims, with representatives of the families and independent pathologists allowed to participate. If criminal negligence, unlawful detention, reckless conduct or any deliberate act contributed to these deaths, those responsible must be prosecuted, irrespective of their rank or position. “This tragedy must also trigger a nationwide review of detention facilities operated by all security agencies to ensure that no Nigerian is ever again placed in a situation where a cry for help becomes a cry that nobody answers.’’ 66 detainees Allied Peoples Movement, APM, alleged that 66 detainees were crammed into a cell, adding that 37 subsequently died from excessive heat. In a statement by its National Publicity Secretary, Yusuf Abubakar, the party also claimed that some detainees were sprayed with an unidentified substance before some of them collapsed. The APM condemned what it described as inhuman detention conditions and called for an open, transparent and unrestricted investigation into the deaths. It also frowned at the reported use of tear gas and ammunition by security personnel during protests over the incident. “The lives of citizens must be treated with dignity as guaranteed by the 1999 Constitution (as amended). The death of citizens in detention facilities cannot be justified under any guise,” the party said. Wider probe Also, the Media for Social Change Foundation has called for transparent investigations into recent mining-related deaths in Kogi and Taraba states, in addition to the Niger State deaths. The foundation, in a statement jointly signed by its Co-Founders, Boluwaji Obahopo and Opeyemi Owoeye, expressed concern over reports of the deaths of more than 20 miners in separate pit collapses in Kogi and Taraba, as well as the reported deaths of the 37 suspected illegal miners in NSCDC custody in Niger. It said the incidents should prompt authorities to look beyond the familiar issues of illegal mining, enforcement and regulation and examine the conditions exposing miners and mining communities to danger. “A miner should not have to choose between risking death inside a mining pit and risking his life in the course of government enforcement,” the foundation said. On the Niger incident, the organisation described the deaths as particularly disturbing because the victims reportedly died after being taken into custody. It nevertheless acknowledged that the actual cause of the deaths was yet to be established and that forensic examinations and autopsies were being conducted. The foundation urged the authorities to independently and transparently establish the circumstances surrounding the arrests, detention and deaths. “Every death must have an answer. Every answer must lead to accountability where wrongdoing is established,” it said. The organisation called for the findings of investigations into the Kogi, Taraba and Niger incidents to be made public and responsibility established wherever negligence or violations were proven. It also urged authorities to create effective channels through which miners and host communities could report dangerous mining activities and unsafe enforcement practices without fear of reprisals. “No campaign against illegal mining should become a licence for abuse. No mineral is worth a human life,” the foundation said. Apart from growing outrage, the incident also triggered protests in Minna, with security personnel using tear gas to disperse demonstrators who gathered over the deaths. The protests were followed by unrest, prompting the Niger State government to impose a curfew. The protests, which began in Minna on Thursday night and continued on Friday, were reported in Tunga, Maitumbi and along Bosso Road, with youths chanting “Justice must be done” as anger grew over the deaths. The post 37 miners’ suffocation: Anger spreads, 20 security officers suspended, mining disasters rock Kogi, Taraba appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Kohat attack
items.description: FRIDAY’S attack in Kohat marks a further escalation by Pakistan’s enemies. They targeted a mosque in Kohat’s old Police Lines with an explosives-laden vehicle, then attempted to storm the compound and attack police facilities in the ensuing chaos. At least 23, including 17 police personnel and officials, were martyred in this dastardly assault on worshippers. More than 100 were wounded. But police and security forces regrouped quickly and launched a valiant counterassault, eliminating all but two of the attackers within hours of the initial bombing. The remaining two were neutralised in a clean-up operation that extended overnight, supervised by some of the top police and counterterrorism officials, with one holed-up terrorist killed and the other blowing themselves up rather than face the consequences of their actions. The operation produced considerable acts of courage, not least by the additional inspector-general of the CTD, who was injured by a grenade yet returned to conclude the clean-up. The nation will mourn the lives lost and pray for those who were injured. The nation will also demand swift justice for those who lost loved ones. The group which claimed the attack has, by attacking worshippers on what Muslims consider the holiest occasion of the week, not only shown that it observes no ethical limits, but also that it is operating with a single goal: to cause maximum bloodshed and harm. The Ittehadul Mujahideen, an umbrella organisation of terrorist outfits, is, according to the Jamestown Foundation think tank, believed to operate from safe havens across the border, share intelligence and coordinate attacks with its terrorist factions, and run organised digital campaigns. It has apparently used drone technologies to deadly effect while targeting security forces and installations in the past. As such, it is considered in some circles to be a more serious and sophisticated threat than the TTP. It needs to be treated as such. The KP police must be better equipped and trained. They are facing an enemy which is increasingly using modern technology to cause bloodshed. They must be supported with the equipment, strategies and technologies they need to effectively limit and counter the constant, deadly threat they face. Simultaneously, the authorities need to review the approaches being taken to counter violent actors. National policy on counterterrorism requires recalibration and revisiting, especially regarding its diplomatic, political and social aspects, which must be addressed together to secure stable dividends. Sadly, the public’s attention is so fixated on social, political and economic problems that the terrorism crisis has been pushed to the margins of national discourse. Pakistan must confront these networks with the full force of the state and the law, but cannot do so effectively till its own house is in order. Published in Dawn, September 20th, 2026

items.title: CNG: There ‘ll be fare cut from October 1 – Tinubu
items.description: By Johnbosco Agbakwuru President Bola Tinubu has said that from October 1, commuters across Nigeria must begin to see measurable reductions in transportation fares as he has directed all 36 states to accelerate the National Affordable CNG Transit Programme. In a statement personally signed and released on Saturday, September 19, Tinubu said the push followed his August 27 meeting with state governors, where they “agreed on a clear objective: From October 1, more Nigerians should begin to see measurable reductions in transportation costs.” To drive implementation, the President said an implementation committee for the CNG programme was established under the Nigeria Governors’ Forum, chaired by Kwara State Governor and NGF Chairman, AbdulRahman AbdulRazaq. “These are not projections. Nigerians are already experiencing these savings,” he said. Tinubu pointed to existing CNG and electric transport deployments as proof that cheaper energy can immediately translate into lower fares, listing concrete examples across the country: The President said that in Borno State, CNG and electric public transport charge between ₦50 and ₦100 on routes where commercial operators charge ₦300–₦600. In Kaduna: 100 CNG-powered buses provide free transportation on major routes; noting that in their first year they carried about 3.2 million passengers and saved commuters over ₦3.5 billion. He further stated that in Oyo State, CNG buses deployed to Pacesetter Transport cut the Lagos–Ibadan fare from about ₦8,000 to ₦3,200, while in Adamawa, Alternative-energy transit services reduced fares by up to 50 per cent, from ₦8,000 to ₦4,000. Also in Enugu, 100 CNG buses reduced the Enugu–Nsukka fare from ₦2,500 to ₦1,500 and in Plateau, government-supported buses carry about 13,000 commuters daily at ₦200, compared with over ₦500 commercially. Tinubu said in Abuja, in partnership with the National Union of Road Transport Workers, NURTW, CNG-converted commercial vehicles offer a 40 per cent fare reduction on several routes; Area 1–Gwagwalada fell from ₦1,500 to ₦900, Nyanya from ₦700 to ₦420, and Wuse from ₦400 to ₦240. He said in Niger, passengers on the Suleja–Abuja service now pay ₦550 instead of about ₦800, while in Abia, 40 electric buses have been deployed with fares subsidised by 50 per cent. “These are not projections. Nigerians are already experiencing these savings,” Tinubu said. “Our answer cannot be to return to the ruinous petrol subsidy regime” Acknowledging renewed pressure on petrol and diesel prices from global energy disruptions, Tinubu stressed that Nigeria cannot control international oil markets but can reduce its exposure by leveraging domestic gas He said his administration has, over the last three years, deliberately built a CNG transportation ecosystem, with more than 120,000 vehicles converted, over 400 certified conversion centres, and more than 90 CNG refuelling stations nationwide—figures he said are increasing daily. “At a time like this, our answer cannot be to return to the ruinous petrol subsidy regime that consumed trillions of naira and left our economy exposed to every movement in international oil prices, as some have suggested,” he said. “We must accelerate the cheaper alternatives we have been building at home.” “I commend the Governors… However, more still needs to be done” Tinubu commended states that have moved quickly, citing active CNG bus services in Edo (50 buses), over 1,000 converted commercial vehicles in Kano, expanding CNG-supported services in Delta, Kwara and Lagos, and Akwa Ibom’s receipt of 50 CNG buses ahead of commercial operations. But he warned that more must be done, urging every state to “maintain the momentum towards October 1.” “Work with transport unions and commercial operators. Support conversion and fleet deployment. Facilitate the infrastructure required. Above all, ensure that savings from cheaper energy reach Nigerian citizens through lower fares,” he said. “Nigeria has the gas. We are building the infrastructure. We are already seeing the savings.” The President pledged continued federal support to scale CNG infrastructure and access, expand conversion capacity, and create an enabling environment for states, transport operators, manufacturers and private investors to participate. “Nigeria has the gas. We are building the infrastructure. We are already seeing the savings,” Tinubu said. “Now we must move faster and scale this so that more Nigerians feel those savings in the fares they pay every day.” The post CNG: There ‘ll be fare cut from October 1 – Tinubu appeared first on Vanguard News .
